result:
Thanks. That's the full picture of what you want. One quick step before I write: you choose how it gets built. That choice changes most of the document. Here are the three real options:

1. **Add it to the taproom app.** New pages and tables go into the existing Flask app and its SQLite database on the Pi.
   - Good: the least work, with one thing to run and back up.
   - Cost: tabs and trace records share one database. A bad taproom change could damage brewing records.
2. **Build a separate small app on the same Pi (my recommendation).** It uses the same tools (Flask and SQLite) but has its own database file.
   - Good: the brewery floor and the taproom can't break each other. You can back up the trace records on their own and keep them for years.
   - Cost: a second service to keep running on the Pi. That's a small load.
3. **Buy hosted brewery software,** such as Ekos or Breww.
   - Good: nothing to build.
   - Cost: a monthly fee, and scanning on the floor depends on the internet. It also won't fit the way you described your sacks and labels without some workarounds.

I recommend option 2. A recall trace is the one record you can't lose. Keeping it apart from the daily tab traffic protects it, and it adds almost no work.

After you pick, I'll write the full design into `specs/`. A reviewer will read it first. I may come back once with a few questions, but only ones that change what gets built. This folder isn't under git yet, so I'll set that up when I commit the spec.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- SQLite keeps each database in a single file. With a separate file, a backup of the trace records is just a copy of that file.
- A USB barcode scanner usually acts like a keyboard. Scanned sack lots can go into a normal web form field, so the scanning works the same with any of these options.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Which of the three do you want?
